CHAPTER 7.3 · LEARNING AREA 7

CHAPTER 7.3 · LEARNING AREA 7 · JANUARY

Distances

How high is a pyramid above its base, how far does an antenna stick out above the roof, when does a drone reach the wall of a house? All of these are questions about distances. You calculate the distance between two points, find the nearest point of a plane with the perpendicular line and use the Hesse normal form as a shortcut. At the end you draw up your own solution plans for problems from architecture and engineering.

8 LESSONS2 UNITS3 WIDGETS1 LAB
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • calculate the distance between two points as the length of the connecting vector
  • use the perpendicular line to find the foot of the perpendicular and the distance from a point to a plane
  • apply the distance formula with the normal vector and tell which side of the plane a point is on
  • calculate distances and angles on solids and in applications with a solution plan

UNIT 14 LESSONS

1Distances between points and from points to planes

The distance between two points is the length of their connecting vector. The question of how far a point $P$ is from a plane is harder: the plane has infinitely many points. The nearest one is the foot of the perpendicular $F$, because the shortest connection is perpendicular to the plane, so it runs in the direction of the normal vector.

You set up the perpendicular line through $P$ with the direction vector $\vec n$ and intersect it with the plane. The parameter $t$ of the point of intersection also gives you the distance straight away: $d = |t| \cdot |\vec n|$. Combining the calculation gives a formula for which you do not need the foot of the perpendicular at all. In addition, the sign inside the absolute value shows which side of the plane the point lies on.

KEY POINT · DISTANCES

Point and point: $d(P, Q) = |\vec{PQ}| = \sqrt{(q_1 - p_1)^2 + (q_2 - p_2)^2 + (q_3 - p_3)^2}$

Foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to $E\colon \vec n \circ \vec x = d$: substitute the perpendicular line $\vec x = \vec p + t \cdot \vec n$ into $E$, find $t$, work out $F$.

Distance formula: $d(P, E) = \dfrac{|\vec n \circ \vec p - d|}{|\vec n|}$ · Same sign of $\vec n \circ \vec p - d$: same side of the plane.

Hesse normal form: If you divide the coordinate equation by $|\vec n|$, i.e. $\tfrac{1}{|\vec n|}(\vec n \circ \vec x - d) = 0$, substituting a point gives its distance with a sign directly.

Parallel planes with the same $\vec n$: $d = \tfrac{|d_1 - d_2|}{|\vec n|}$.

Two points, their connecting vector, its length and the midpoint. Dragging rotates the coordinate system.

INTERACTIVE · THE PERPENDICULAR TO THE PLANE

Enter a plane and a point: the widget sets up the perpendicular line, finds the foot of the perpendicular $F$ and the distance in both ways. You will need the mirror point in Chapter 8.1.

EXAMPLE 1 · TWO POINTS

How far apart are $A(2, -1, 3)$ and $B(4, 1, 4)$, and where is the midpoint of the line segment?

$\vec{AB} = (2, 2, 1)$, $|\vec{AB}| = \sqrt{4 + 4 + 1} = 3$.

$d = 3$, $M(3, 0, 3.5)$

EXAMPLE 2 · FOOT OF THE PERPENDICULAR AND DISTANCE

Find the foot of the perpendicular from $P(4, 3, 2)$ to $E\colon 2x + y + 2z = 6$ and the distance.

Perpendicular line $(4 + 2t, 3 + t, 2 + 2t)$ in $E$: $15 + 9t = 6$, $t = -1$, so $F(2, 2, 0)$.

$d = |t| \cdot |\vec n| = 3$. Check with the formula: $\tfrac{|15 - 6|}{3} = 3$ ✔

EXERCISES

Calculate the distances: a) $(1, 2, 3)$ and $(3, 4, 4)$   b) $(2, 3, 6)$ from the origin.

a) $\sqrt{4 + 4 + 1} = 3$   b) $\sqrt{49} = 7$

Calculate with the distance formula: a) $O$ from $2x + y + 2z = 6$   b) $(1, 1, 1)$ from $2x - y + 2z = 9$.

a) $\tfrac{6}{3} = 2$   b) $\tfrac{|3 - 9|}{3} = 2$

Which point of the plane $2x + y + 2z = 9$ is nearest to the origin?

Perpendicular line $t \cdot (2, 1, 2)$: $9t = 9$, $t = 1$: $F(2, 1, 2)$, distance $3$.

How far apart are the parallel planes $2x + y + 2z = 3$ and $2x + y + 2z = 12$?

$\tfrac{|12 - 3|}{3} = 3$

Which points of the $z$-axis are at distance $3$ from $E\colon 2x + y + 2z = 6$? On which side of $E$ does each of them lie, compared with the origin?

$\tfrac{|2z - 6|}{3} = 3$: $z = 7.5$ or $z = -1.5$. Sign of $2z - 6$: positive at $7.5$ (other side from $O$, which gives $-6$), negative at $-1.5$ (same side as $O$).

UNIT 24 LESSONS

2Distances and angles in applications

A pyramid has the base $A(0, 0, 0)$, $B(8, 0, 0)$, $C(8, 8, 0)$, $D(0, 8, 0)$ and the apex $S(4, 4, 6)$. Height, edge length, slant height, volume, inclinations, the distance from a corner to the opposite lateral face: each of these quantities is a distance or an angle you can already calculate.

In applied problems the calculation is usually short; the hard part is the translation. A solution plan helps: what are you looking for? Which distance or angle is it, between which objects? Which equations do I need for it, and which are still missing? At the end you check whether the result fits the situation: no roof is $80^\circ$ steep, no antenna sticks out $50$ m above a family house.

KEY POINT · SOLUTION PLAN FOR APPLICATIONS

1. Sketch and coordinates of the points, lines and planes involved.

2. Name the quantity you want: distance point–point, point–plane or an angle of intersection?

3. Set up the missing equations, calculate, add the unit, check the result against the situation.

The height of a pyramid is the distance of the apex from the plane of the base, even if the base is slanted. Volume: $V = \tfrac13 \cdot G \cdot h$.

Motion: A drone on $\vec x = \vec p + t \cdot \vec v$ is at the point $\vec p + t \vec v$ at time $t$. Distances then change with $t$; more on this in Chapter 8.1.

INTERACTIVE · PYRAMID AND PRISM

Change the base and the apex. The widget calculates the volume and the lateral surface with the vector product. What role does the distance of the apex from the base play?

EXAMPLE 3 · MEASURING A PYRAMID

The pyramid from the introduction: calculate the volume, the edge length $|\vec{AS}|$ and the distance from $A$ to the lateral face $BCS$.

Height $6$: $V = \tfrac13 \cdot 64 \cdot 6 = 128$. $\vec{AS} = (4, 4, 6)$, $|\vec{AS}| = \sqrt{68} \approx 8.25$.

$\vec{BC} \times \vec{BS} = (48, 0, 32)$, so $BCS\colon 3x + 2z = 24$. $d(A, BCS) = \tfrac{24}{\sqrt{13}} \approx 6.66$

EXAMPLE 4 · ANTENNA ABOVE THE ROOF

A roof surface lies in $3y + 4z = 24$ (in m, $z$ upwards). How far is the tip of the antenna $(3, 5, 7)$ from the roof surface, and where does the perpendicular meet the roof?

$d = \tfrac{|15 + 28 - 24|}{5} = \tfrac{19}{5} = 3.8$ m. Perpendicular line $(3, 5 + 3t, 7 + 4t)$: $43 + 25t = 24$, $t = -0.76$.

$3.8$ m, foot of the perpendicular $(3, 2.72, 3.96)$

EXERCISES

What is the longest straight pole that fits into a room $5$ m long, $4$ m wide and $3$ m high?

Space diagonal $\sqrt{25 + 16 + 9} = \sqrt{50} \approx 7.07$ m

Does the sphere with centre $M(1, 1, 1)$ and radius $1$ touch the plane $2x + y + 2z = 8$?

$d(M, E) = \tfrac{|5 - 8|}{3} = 1 = r$: yes, the plane touches the sphere.

A tetrahedron has the corners $O$, $(3, 0, 0)$, $(0, 3, 0)$, $(0, 0, 3)$. Calculate the height above the slanted base, the area of the base and the volume.

Base in $x + y + z = 3$: $h = \tfrac{3}{\sqrt3} = \sqrt3$. $G = \tfrac12 |(-3, 3, 0) \times (-3, 0, 3)| = \tfrac92\sqrt3$. $V = \tfrac13 \cdot \tfrac92\sqrt3 \cdot \sqrt3 = 4.5$ ✔

A mast $30$ m high stands at the origin; a cable runs from the top to the ground point $(20, 15, 0)$. How long is the cable, and what angle does it make with the ground?

$\sqrt{400 + 225 + 900} \approx 39.1$ m. Horizontally $25$ m, $\tan\varphi = \tfrac{30}{25}$: $\varphi \approx 50.2^\circ$.

A drone flies along $\vec x = (0, 0, 10) + t \cdot (4, 3, 0)$ ($t$ in s, lengths in m) towards the wall of a house $E\colon 3x + 4y = 200$. How far is it from the wall after $5$ s? When does it reach the wall?

After $5$ s at $(20, 15, 10)$: $d = \tfrac{|60 + 60 - 200|}{5} = 16$ m. Substituting: $24t = 200$, after about $8.3$ s.

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

Which point of the $x$-axis is the same distance from $A(1, 1, 0)$ and $B(3, -1, 2)$?

$(x - 1)^2 + 1 = (x - 3)^2 + 1 + 4$ gives $x = 3$: $(3, 0, 0)$, both distances $\sqrt5$.

Connecting with Chapter 7.2: For the pyramid from Example 3, find the inclination of the lateral faces and of the lateral edges to the base.

Lateral face: height $6$ above half the side $4$, $\tan\varphi = 1.5$, $\varphi \approx 56.3^\circ$. Edge: $\sin\varphi = \tfrac{6}{\sqrt{68}}$, $\varphi \approx 46.7^\circ$.

Do $O$ and $Q(3, 3, 3)$ lie on the same side of $E\colon 2x + y + 2z = 6$? Justify with the Hesse normal form.

$\tfrac13 (0 - 6) = -2$ and $\tfrac13 (15 - 6) = 3$: different signs, so different sides. The line segment $OQ$ pierces $E$.

Show that $g\colon \vec x = (1, 1, 5) + t(1, 0, -1)$ is parallel to $E\colon x + y + z = 1$, and calculate the distance from $g$ to $E$.

$(1, 0, -1) \circ (1, 1, 1) = 0$: parallel. All points of $g$ are the same distance away, so one point is enough: $\tfrac{|7 - 1|}{\sqrt3} = 2\sqrt3 \approx 3.46$.

EXCURSIONTECHNOLOGY

Distances make the position: GPS

A GPS receiver in a phone does not measure directions, only times. The satellites orbit about $20{,}200$ km above the Earth and constantly send their exact time and position. The travel time of a signal gives the distance to the satellite: light covers roughly $300$ m in one microsecond. A known distance to one satellite means the receiver lies on a sphere around it. Two spheres intersect in a circle, three in two points.

There is a catch: the clock in the receiver is not accurate enough. Its error is a fourth unknown next to the three coordinates. That is why the receiver needs the signals of at least four satellites to find the four unknowns. Even the theory of relativity has to be taken into account: the clocks in the satellites run about $38$ microseconds per day faster than on Earth.

Source: Wikipedia (English), article “Global Positioning System”.
